newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania struggles to reassert order after PM ambush.
newsitem.headline: Albania struggles to reassert order after PM ambush.

text.p: Albanian authorities struggled to reassert control on Sunday after gunmen ambushed Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, underscoring continuing lawlessness in the Balkan state as it awaits deployment of an Italian-led security force.

Martin Gjoni, police chief in the northern town of Shkoder, said he had identified many of the grenade-throwing gang who barred a road north of Tirana to a convoy of cars carrying Fino and other ministers on Saturday and forced them to turn back.

"I know many of them and I will send them to trial for this ugly act," Gjoni told Albanian television. But there were no immediate reports of arrests after the roadside hold-up by about 15 gunmen, in which no one was hurt.

The formerly Stalinist country slid towards anarchy last month after protests at the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes spilled over into insurrection. Many weapons depots have been looted and banditry is rife.
Shkoder, which Fino had planned to visit, was calm on Sunday. "All the forces in Shkoder support Mr Fino's government," right-wing mayor Bahri Borici told Reuters.
But the attack caused political strains in Fino's fractious all-party coalition appointed at the height of unrest on March 11. Fino is aiming to restore order and prepare June elections.
Fino is an economist from southern Albania, where many towns are controlled by rebel councils demanding the resignation of right-wing President Sali Berisha, a northerner.

Gjoni said the gunmen, who detonated two grenades by the roadside and fired shots in the air, were demanding the release of 120 people from the Shkoder region they alleged were held in the southern, rebel-held port of Sarande.
The Sarande council denied the charge and accused extremists of wanting to split Albania in two.

Rivalries have long existed between the poorer, mountainous north and the south of Europe's most impoverished country, but many Albanians say they do not run deep enough to cause a rift in the tiny country of 3.4 million people.

Shkoder mayor Borici said he had been looking forward to Fino's visit to discuss problems such as unpaid pensions and welfare. Pope John Paul visited Shkoder in 1993 and said mass in its cathedral, used as a sports hall during communist rule.
The attack on Fino illustrated the extent of lawlessness in the country, awaiting the arrival of a U.N.-approved force of up to 6,000 troops to protect shipments of food and medicines.

Italy, which says the force will start to arrive in the week of April 14, is expected to provide 2,000 to 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. Austria and Denmark may also take part.
Italy has become Albania's closest economic partner since the Cold War after a history that has swung between aid and aggression.
April 7th is the 58th anniversary of an invasion of Albania by Benito Mussolini's fascist Italy, a few months before the start of World War Two in 1939.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has called in parliamentary party leaders of his alliance to talks on Monday ahead of votes on the force this week. A key ally is opposed, forcing him to rely on votes from opposition parties favouring deployment.
